blocks.content: A design that only works for today's requirements is fragile the moment a new requirement shows up next month.
Extensibility is the property of a design that lets new behavior get added without reopening and re-testing code that already worked.
This lesson looks at what extensibility actually means in practice, concrete ways to build it in, and the honest balance against overengineering that this course covered earlier.
An extensible design lets you add new behavior by writing new code, not by editing code that already worked.
1. What Extensibility Actually Means
A useful test is imagining a new requirement arriving tomorrow, then asking how many existing files would need to change to satisfy it.
Extensibility is often described vaguely as flexible or easy to change. A more precise definition helps.
A design is extensible for a specific kind of change if that change can be made by adding new code alongside the existing code, rather than editing the existing code.
Extensible for what, specifically
No design is extensible for every possible future change. A good design is deliberately extensible for the changes that are actually likely, and accepts that unlikely changes may need real rework.

["A payment system is usually extensible for new payment methods, since new ones appear regularly.","That same system is rarely designed to be extensible for switching its entire currency model, since that almost never happens."]
items: A payment system is usually extensible for new payment methods, since new ones appear regularly.
That same system is rarely designed to be extensible for switching its entire currency model, since that almost never happens.

blocks.title: Extensibility is always scoped
blocks.content: Asking "extensible for what change" is more useful than asking "is this extensible" as a yes or no question.
Extensibility versus flexibility
Flexibility is a vague feeling, extensibility is a concrete, checkable property of a specific extension point.
You can point at exactly which class or interface a new payment method needs to implement, and confirm nothing else needs touching.
2. A Rigid Design That Resists Change
blocks.text: 2. A Rigid Design That Resists Change

blocks.content: It helps to see what rigidity looks like concretely before looking at the fix, since the fix only makes sense once the pain is visible.
The most common rigid shape is a long if-else or switch chain that branches on some kind of type field.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512480128-290878333.png
blocks.alt: A rigid charge method branching on payment method type, where adding a new type means editing the shared method

blocks.content: Adding cryptocurrency support means finding this method, adding another branch, and retesting the entire method, including the branches that had nothing to do with the change.
Why this gets worse over time
blocks.text: Why this gets worse over time

blocks.content: Every new payment method adds one more branch, and the method grows a little riskier to touch each time.
Eventually a small addition, like a sixth payment method, carries the same review burden as a change to the whole class.
The specific risk of editing shared code
blocks.text: The specific risk of editing shared code

blocks.content: Every edit to this one method risks a typo or a logic slip that affects every payment method, not just the new one being added.
A test suite covering all six branches has to pass again after every single addition, even though five of those branches did not change at all.
3. Extension Points Through Interfaces
This is the single most common technique for extensibility across nearly every mainstream language.
An extension point is a well defined seam in the design where new behavior can be plugged in without touching what already exists.
The classic way to create one is an interface, or an abstract class, that new behavior implements.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512482096-762211559.png
blocks.alt: A PaymentMethod interface as the extension point, with CardPayment and PaypalPayment implementing it and a new CryptoPayment added alongside

blocks.content: The processor no longer branches
The processor now only knows about the PaymentMethod shape, never about any specific concrete method.
Where the branch went
The branching logic did not disappear, it moved into a lookup on a map, which is data rather than code.
Adding a new entry to that lookup is a much smaller, safer change than adding a new branch to a growing conditional.
4. Plugin Style Registration
An extension point alone is only half the picture, the system also needs a way to discover and use whatever implements it.
Once new behavior lives behind an interface, it needs to be registered somewhere so the system knows it exists.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512483626-825384182.png
blocks.alt: A registration list mapping payment method names to implementations, where adding crypto is a single new line

blocks.content: A simple registry
This registry is exactly the composition root idea from the Inversion of Control lesson, one place allowed to know about every concrete implementation.
Framework level plugin systems
Many real frameworks take this further, scanning a folder or a package for anything matching an extension point and registering it automatically, no manual list required.
Manual registration is still perfectly valid
blocks.text: Manual registration is still perfectly valid

blocks.content: A small to medium codebase does not need automatic discovery, an explicit list of registrations is easier to read and reason about.
Automatic discovery earns its complexity once the number of extensions grows large enough that a manual list becomes tedious to maintain.
5. Composition Over Inheritance for Extensibility
There is a second, closely related technique worth knowing alongside interfaces and registries.
Inheritance can also provide extension points, but it locks a subclass into one fixed parent, which itself can only be swapped by changing the class definition.
Composition, handing in a collaborator object rather than extending a base class, keeps the door open to change that collaborator at runtime.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512485401-283712786.png
blocks.alt: Inheritance locking a class to one fixed parent compared with composition holding a swappable collaborator

A quick example of the difference
blocks.text: A quick example of the difference

blocks.content: A ReportGenerator that extends a base ReportFormatter class can only ever format reports one way, whatever its parent defines.
The same ReportGenerator holding a formatter object passed in through its constructor can format differently for every instance, chosen at construction time.
6. Balancing Extensibility Against Overengineering
Everything so far has been about how to build extensibility. This section is about when it is actually worth building.
This course already covered overengineering in depth, and it applies directly here.
Every extension point is a small amount of permanent complexity, paid whether or not the extension ever actually gets used.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783496492082-811739855.png
blocks.alt: A rigid design where new behavior forces editing existing code, risking what already worked

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783496494003-211461008.png
blocks.alt: An extensible design where new behavior is added as a new class registered alongside existing ones, leaving existing code untouched

blocks.content: A practical filter

["Has this kind of change already happened more than once in this codebase.","Is a second variant already known to be coming, not just hypothetically possible.","Would the extension point actually be simpler than the if-else chain it replaces."]
items: Has this kind of change already happened more than once in this codebase.
Is a second variant already known to be coming, not just hypothetically possible.
Would the extension point actually be simpler than the if-else chain it replaces.

blocks.content: If none of these are true yet, a plain if-else chain is completely reasonable until the pattern of change actually shows up.

blocks.title: Extensibility is earned, not assumed
blocks.content: Build the extension point once you have seen the variation happen at least once, not in anticipation of variation that might never come.
The cost side of the ledger
blocks.text: The cost side of the ledger

blocks.content: An extension point that never gets a second implementation is pure overhead, an interface and a registry serving exactly one concrete class forever.
That overhead is small for one extension point, but it adds up quickly across a codebase full of extension points built speculatively.
7. A Worked Payment Method Refactor
Seeing the whole arc, from rigid to extensible to actually being extended, makes the earlier sections concrete.
Picture a payment system that started with just card and PayPal support, using the rigid if-else version.

blocks.title: The trigger for refactoring
blocks.text: The team is asked to add bank transfer support, and two weeks later, cryptocurrency support. That is the pattern of repeated variation that justifies extracting an extension point.

blocks.content: After the refactor shown earlier in this lesson, adding cryptocurrency support means writing one new CryptoPayment class and one registration line.
No existing test for card or PayPal payments needed to be rerun because of this change, since nothing they depend on was modified.
What the code review looked like
blocks.text: What the code review looked like

blocks.content: The pull request for cryptocurrency support contained exactly one new file and one new line in the registration list.
A reviewer could focus entirely on whether CryptoPayment itself was correct, without needing to re-verify card or PayPal behavior at all.
8. Testing Extensible Designs
Testing turns out to be where extensibility quietly pays off the most, beyond the original goal of adding new behavior easily.
An unexpected benefit of extension points is that each implementation can be tested completely in isolation.
A test for CryptoPayment never needs to construct or mock CardPayment or PaypalPayment, since they live in entirely separate classes.

["Each extension implementation gets its own focused test suite.","The processor itself only needs a test confirming it dispatches to the right registered implementation.","A fake implementation of the extension point makes testing the processor trivial, no real payment gateway needed."]
items: Each extension implementation gets its own focused test suite.
The processor itself only needs a test confirming it dispatches to the right registered implementation.
A fake implementation of the extension point makes testing the processor trivial, no real payment gateway needed.

blocks.content: 9. Closing: Extensibility Is a Deliberate Choice
blocks.text: 9. Closing: Extensibility Is a Deliberate Choice

blocks.content: Extensibility is not a property you get by trying hard to write flexible code from day one.
It is a property that shows up when a specific, well scoped seam has been deliberately placed exactly where real variation actually occurs.
It comes from noticing where change actually happens repeatedly, and deliberately carving out an extension point right there, while leaving the rest of the system as simple and direct as it can be.
A short checklist to carry forward
blocks.text: A short checklist to carry forward

blocks.content: ["Has this exact kind of change already happened more than once here.","Would a new extension point replace something more complex than it adds.","Can the extension be tested completely on its own, without touching existing tests.","Is there exactly one place responsible for wiring new extensions in."]
items: Has this exact kind of change already happened more than once here.
Would a new extension point replace something more complex than it adds.
Can the extension be tested completely on its own, without touching existing tests.
Is there exactly one place responsible for wiring new extensions in.

blocks.content: Answering these honestly, case by case, keeps a codebase extensible where it matters and simple everywhere else.

blocks.title: A closing contrast
blocks.text: Team A adds an interface and a registry the moment they write their second payment method. Team B waits for a third payment method request before refactoring. Team B usually ships faster and ends up with a design shaped by real requirements instead of guesses.

blocks.content: The next topic looks at the Open/Closed Principle specifically, the formal name for exactly this idea, open for extension, closed for modification.
Carry the checklist above with you, it applies just as well there as it does here.
Good design here is less about clever abstractions and more about noticing patterns of real change before reacting to them.
That habit of noticing is worth more than any specific pattern covered in this lesson.
Build the seam where change actually happens, not where you imagine it might.
